title: Pyeatte v. Pyeatte
lead: A wife supported her husband through law school under a plan that he would later fund her master’s degree, but their marriage ended before her turn; restitution survived even though the educational promise was too indefinite to enforce.

actors.name: Margrethe May Pyeatte
actors.role: Wife who financed living and educational expenses

actors.name: H. Charles Pyeatte
actors.role: Husband who completed law school before dissolution

actors.name: Judge Corcoran
actors.role: Author of the Arizona appellate opinion

proceedings: Dissolution court awarded $23,000 as contract damages with supervised installments; Court of Appeals rejected contract and property grounds, recognized limited restitution, reversed the amount, and remanded for recalculation.
limits: The degree was not divisible community property. The $23,000 expectation award was not affirmed as restitution. Recovery concerned extraordinary unrecompensed financial support under this agreement, capped by the anticipated reciprocal benefit if smaller.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The spouses planned successive educational opportunities
sections.cue: Introduce the agreement and the support actually supplied.
paragraphs: Margrethe May Pyeatte and H. Charles Pyeatte married in December 1972, each already holding a bachelor’s degree. In early 1974 they agreed that Margrethe would support them during Charles’s three years of law school so he would not need to work, and he would afterward support her through a master’s degree without her working. Charles acknowledged an agreement but disputed its qualifications. The trial court found no express or implied divorce exception.

Margrethe supported the household from salary during the first two law-school years. After losing her job during the final year, they used jointly accumulated savings to which she had contributed significantly. Charles graduated and gained bar admission. They moved to Prescott, where his starting law-firm salary could not support both household costs and her studies. She agreed to postpone schooling one or two years while he established practice and took part-time teaching work.

In April 1978, Charles said he no longer wanted the marriage. Margrethe filed for dissolution in June. At the March 1979 trial, little community property existed, its division was undisputed, and she neither sought nor received maintenance. The marriage ended before her educational turn and before his professional earnings built a substantial estate.

sections.title: The trial court valued the education Margrethe had expected
sections.cue: Distinguish that original award from the eventual restitution inquiry.
paragraphs: The trial court treated the arrangement as an enforceable contract, found Margrethe performed and Charles did not, and awarded $23,000 based on expert estimates of her proposed education’s cost. It required quarterly payments of at least ten percent of his net income, income-generating efforts and records, access to those records, and continuing supervision.

Charles appealed. Margrethe defended through contract, the statutory property-division power, and unjust enrichment. Judge Corcoran’s appellate opinion considered those grounds separately rather than treating failure of the contract as decisive of every possible remedy.

sections.title: The reciprocal promise lacked essential boundaries, and the degree was not property
sections.cue: Explain why the first two theories failed.
paragraphs: The court accepted that the spouses had an understanding and did not categorically reject agreements between spouses. But Margrethe’s educational entitlement lacked sufficient definition. Unlike Charles’s specified three law-school years, her program had no settled start, duration, institution, location, relocation obligation, or spending level. An inexpensive local course and a costly out-of-state program would impose materially different duties. Those deficiencies made it unnecessary to resolve Charles’s argument about divorce.

Courts preferred interpretations preserving agreements, and performance mattered, but interpretation could not become creation of essential commitments the parties never settled. Margrethe’s support did not authorize the court to supply the entire reciprocal arrangement.

Nor could the court treat Charles’s degree, license, or enhanced earning capacity as community property under Arizona Revised Statutes § 25-318. Wisner, an earlier education-and-property decision, rejected that classification. References to education as an economically valuable marital asset did not make it legally divisible property or support the requested statutory lien or reimbursement.

sections.title: The failed bargain still explained why retention could be unjust
sections.cue: Identify the narrow circumstances beyond ordinary marital contributions.
paragraphs: The arrangement remained evidence that Margrethe expected reciprocal educational assistance rather than making a purely gratuitous contribution. Her payments relieved Charles of living and educational expenses so he could study without working, delay, or additional borrowing. Restitution addressed unjust retention of that benefit; an implied-in-fact contract would still face the same missing definiteness and could not be created by relabeling the bargain.

The court distinguished Wisner’s general reluctance to account for contributions within an ongoing marriage. Ordinary reciprocal household efforts are consumed within the relationship, not converted to invoices on divorce. Wisner involved a long marriage, significant enjoyment of professional earnings, and property and maintenance awards. Here support was concentrated and substantially unilateral, little property accumulated, and dissolution followed professional training before planned reciprocity.

Those facts, including the agreement, justified a limited personal restitution obligation. The court declined to decide standards without an agreement and rejected treating every marriage as an enterprise requiring reimbursement of every contribution. Cases involving substantial returns already enjoyed through marriage or property division therefore differed.

sections.title: The remand replaced expectation damages with a capped benefit calculation
sections.cue: Preserve both the ceiling and flexible payment authority.
paragraphs: The $23,000 measured the promised cost of Margrethe’s education, not automatically the benefit Charles should restore. The trial court needed to determine unjust enrichment and her financial contributions to his living and direct educational expenses. Recovery could not exceed the reciprocal benefit she expected if that amount was smaller than her contribution; restitution could not give her a better financial return than the planned exchange.

The court approved equitable flexibility to permit periodic payments, interest, and appropriate review of income records. Charles could instead pay a lump sum, and installments accommodating his finances did not invalidate otherwise proper relief. That authority did not reinstate the original amount or prescribe a uniform schedule for every educational-support case.

On October 28, 1982, Corcoran, Froeb, and Hathaway reversed the $23,000 portion and remanded for proceedings consistent with that restitution analysis. No separate opinion was reported. The court neither priced the degree as divisible property nor ordered specific performance of the indefinite promise to fund a master’s program.
